interest: This file provides valuable historical insight into the nexus of maritime choke-points, clandestine intelligence collection, and global Axis diplomacy in the prelude to the Pacific War. It uniquely demonstrates how Japanese consular personnel stationed at the Suez Canal engaged in direct military reconnaissance—such as photographing Allied airfield infrastructure—while simultaneously functioning as an intelligence hub linking Tokyo, Europe, and South America. The embedded counter-espionage report detailing secret consultations between Japanese diplomats and former Peruvian Prime Minister José de la Riva-Agüero sheds light on Japan's broader grand strategy to undermine United States influence in the Western Hemisphere and the Pan-American Conference at Lima. Furthermore, the routing of these reports to ONI, MID, and the U.S. Embassy in Lima in late December 1941 highlights the scramble by American intelligence to synthesize pre-war Middle Eastern surveillance into a comprehensive picture of worldwide Axis subversive operations.
overview: This State Department file (decimal file 894.20283) documents Japanese intelligence gathering, military espionage, and political intrigues centered around the Suez Canal Zone in Egypt between 1939 and 1941, along with their wider geopolitical ramifications. Communications from the American Legation in Cairo detail the February 1941 arrest of Japanese Consul Shigeru Tada by Egyptian Coast Guard authorities for photographing military landing field construction near Suez, an episode that precipitated the Egyptian government's closure of foreign consulates across the Canal Zone, before Tada resurfaced attached to Foreign Minister Matsuoka's entourage in Berlin and Rome. The file also contains a 1939 counter-espionage report forwarded from Port Said uncovering Japanese efforts to cultivate Suez Canal Company officials with gifts and detailing confidential discussions with former Peruvian Prime Minister José de la Riva-Agüero aboard the Yasukuni Maru aimed at undermining American influence in Latin America. Transmitted by the State Department to the Military Intelligence Division, the Office of Naval Intelligence, and the U.S. Embassy in Lima in late December 1941, the bundle reflects Allied tracking of Japanese global subversion across the Middle East and the Americas.

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting the arrest and brief detention of the Japanese Consul at Port Said for photographing a military airfield under construction near Suez.
subfiles.summary: American Minister Bert Fish reports that the American Consul at Port Said notified the Legation of the arrest of the Japanese Consul by Egyptian Coast Guard officers approximately thirty kilometers from Suez, south of the El Kabret Peninsula. The Japanese Consul was caught taking photographs of ongoing ground levelling and asphalting operations for an airfield landing strip. The Suez police confiscated his camera film, and the consul was presumed released once his identity was established.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2332 from Cairo on Espionage Activities by the Japanese Consul at Port Said

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a Cairo despatch regarding espionage activities by Japanese Consul Shigeru Tada at Port Said.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference sheet indexes Despatch No. 2368 sent by Raymond A. Hare from Egypt on March 6, 1941. The original document, catalogued under European War file 740.0011 E.W. 1939/10266, discusses espionage activities carried out by Mr. Shigeru Tada, the Japanese Consul at Port Said.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 2368 on Espionage of Shigeru Tada

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting that former consul Shigeru Tada had joined Foreign Minister Matsuoka's mission to Rome and Berlin after being expelled from the Canal Zone.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference sheet references Telegram No. 351 from Alexander C. Kirk in Cairo dated April 27, 1941. It records that former Japanese Consul at Port Said Shigeru Tada, whose illicit activities partly caused the Egyptian government to close all foreign consular posts in the Canal Zone, was attached to Foreign Minister Yōsuke Matsuoka's entourage during his visits to Rome and Berlin. The original telegram was filed under 740.0011 European War 1939/10389.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Telegram No. 351 on Shigeru Tada in Matsuoka's Suite

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet referencing an earlier Cairo despatch concerning Japanese espionage operations in the Suez Canal Zone.
subfiles.summary: This sheet cross-references Despatch No. 2326, forwarded by U.S. Minister Bert Fish from Cairo on February 5, 1941. The underlying communication, located in file 740.00118 European War 1939/188, transmits information concerning Japanese espionage activities across the Suez Canal Zone.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 2326 on Japanese Espionage in Suez Canal Zone

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting a 1939 intelligence report and detailing Japanese efforts to cultivate Suez Canal Company officials through gifts.
subfiles.from: B. Reath Riggs (American Consulate, Port Said)
subfiles.summary: American Consul B. Reath Riggs transmits a confidential report originally prepared in March 1939 by an intelligence agent, brought back to light by the recent 1941 border hostilities between Peru and Ecuador. Riggs recounts that the former Japanese Consul in Port Said had assiduously cultivated Georges Douin, Chef du Transit of the Suez Canal Company, by presenting him with valuable Japanese carved ivories and porcelain figurines for his private collection. The dispatch observes that Douin, a senior official under Baron de Benoist, subsequently declared for General de Gaulle after Allied forces entered Syria.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 123 from Port Said on Japanese Intrigues and Canal Officials

subfiles.about: Intelligence report by an Allied agent on secret meetings between the Japanese Consul at Port Said and former Peruvian Prime Minister José de la Riva-Agüero.
subfiles.summary: An agent embedded within the Japanese Consulate in Port Said reports on the March 16, 1939 arrival of the Japanese liner Yasukuni Maru, carrying former Prime Minister of Peru José de la Riva-Agüero on a tour from Callao via Japan. Guided by Chancellor Tanabe and accompanied by his Swiss secretary, Riva-Agüero held extended secret discussions behind locked doors with Japanese Consul Masato Ohno, who presented the informant as his trusted confidant. The informant indicates that Japan and Germany are working to counter American democratic influence in South America and affect the Lima Conference, and were exploring whether Riva-Agüero would return to political power following lectures in Egypt and Italy.
subfiles.title: Enclosure to Despatch No. 123: Counter-Espionage Report on Riva-Agüero and Japanese Intrigues

subfiles.about: State Department transmittal slip routing Port Said Despatch No. 123 to U.S. military and naval intelligence services.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State formally transmits copies of strictly confidential Despatch No. 123 of August 3, 1941, from Port Said to the Military Intelligence Division (MID) and the Office of Naval Intelligence (ONI). Transmitted three weeks after the Pearl Harbor attack, the routing slip reflects heightened inter-agency intelligence coordination regarding Japanese foreign intrigue and espionage networks.
subfiles.title: State Department Transmittal Slip Distributing Despatch No. 123 to MID and ONI
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division and Office of Naval Intelligence

subfiles.about: Diplomatic instruction transmitting Port Said Despatch No. 123 to the U.S. Ambassador in Lima for information and comment.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull transmits a copy of Port Said Despatch No. 123 and its enclosed counter-espionage report to the American Ambassador in Lima, Peru, for confidential evaluation and comment. Dispatched shortly after the outbreak of the Pacific War, the instruction aims to apprise U.S. diplomats in Peru of historical Japanese political intrigues involving prominent Peruvian figures such as José de la Riva-Agüero.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 806 to the American Ambassador in Lima Transmitting Despatch No. 123
